e13-emuA: I’m well aware that these will often overlap, and that if I talk about jealousy here, it’s likely I should talk about it in regard to all these categories. And even though it all bleeds together in practice, I find that breaking it down like this is a good way to see if there are holes in what a community is doing, because there are so many aspects to communal life.
e13-emuB: I know that a lot of these things will often be interconnected, and aspects of jealousy, resource control, medicine, childrearing, and any other of the items in those boxes will bleed into eachother, but I find it useful to compartmentalize them to some extent to make sure that no area is overlooked when I'm thinking about how a community might function.
e14-emuA:
It doesn’t matter how beautiful the land is if people aren’t clear on who owns it. It doesn’t matter how well-trained the peer counselors are if the membership process admits members too quickly. It doesn’t matter how much medicine the community buys if there’s no written agreement on who has to pay when someone leaves.

These first three parts of a community container are internal.
e14-emuB:
No amount of beautiful land can fix the problems of unclear land ownership. No amount of peer counseling experience can help the people who a group agrees to admit faster than it can support. And no amount of medicine can fix the problem of no written exit agreement.

These first three parts are the container for the rest of the work.
e15-emuA:
If you’re doing a form of reparenting with your inner child, you have to do it by identifying as your inner adult, actually all three of your inner adults. It’s your inner adult that reparents your inner child, not the other way around. It’s your inner nurturing adult, your inner protecting adult, and your inner guru/leader that is responsible for loving, protecting, guiding, and freeing your inner child alive within you.

- Somatic ways of regulating your nervous system

- A contemplative practice informed by the early suttas of Buddhism. However, I approach them critically. I think not all of the early suttas are actually early. They appear to be late additions to the early sutta canon. I also think that the Abhidhamma is a scholastic wrong turn away from the early suttas. I think it’s healthy for any religious community to have a critical relationship to its scriptures.
e15-emuB:
The main difference is that in reparenting you identify with the inner adult, i.e. you are the adult, reparenting your inner child. Of course there are 3 inner adults: inner Nurturer, inner Protector, and inner Guru/Leader.

- Somatic work to regulate the nervous system

My contemplative practice is mostly based on the early Buddhist suttas, but I don’t accept them uncritically. Many are clearly treasures but some appear to be late additions. I see the Abhidhamma as a scholastic wrong turn. A healthy living tradition should be able to hold the relationship of loving what it has received but also being able to disagree.
e16-emuA:
The capacity to be helpful is distributed among the community as a whole, and not contained in any single professional, guru, or emotionally indispensable founder.

The person who is caring for someone does not have jurisdiction over that person’s membership, work, housing, children, medicine, or other evidence. Allowing emotional access to become administrative authority in this way creates a hierarchy that stands in opposition to peer support.

The peer knows what issues are outside of their competence and knows how to seek outside and/or expert assistance when needed.
e16-emuB:
The capacity to provide this kind of help is present in the group, not in any one individual, not in a "professional," not in a "guru," not in the emotionally necessary founder of the group.

This care does not include in any way the power to determine a person's membership in a group, his or her work assignment, his or her housing assignment, the custody of his or her children, the provision of medical care, or other "evidence" of a dispute. This is to avoid any temptation on the part of peers to use their emotional access to create a new form of hierarchy.
